claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
The alloy contains elements such as Al and Ti together with a small Mg addition.
Annealing at 700–750°C accelerates diffusion-driven elemental partitioning.
Annealing at 700–750°C promotes partitioning of Mg into newly formed intermetallic phases.
Service-regime annealing produces discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich precipitates alter local elemental distributions and crystallographic order in the matrix.
Formation of Mg-rich intermetallics depletes the surrounding matrix of elements needed for corrosion inhibition and protective-scale formation.
Matrix depletion caused by precipitation interferes with the continuity and adhesion of the protective oxide layer.
The resulting oxide-scale disruption degrades corrosion resistance.
The resulting oxide-scale disruption degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Annealing near 600°C maintains a metastable homogeneous solid solution.
Retention of the homogeneous solid solution near 600°C preserves corrosion and oxidation protection.
Relative to the initial state, samples annealed at 700–750°C will have a significant increase in the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics.
The increase in Mg-rich intermetallic volume fraction will correlate with reduced corrosion resistance.
The increase in Mg-rich intermetallic volume fraction will correlate with reduced high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Samples annealed near 600°C will retain a homogeneous microstructure and protective oxide properties.
The initial metastable solid-solution state has a uniform, protective oxide layer under service conditions.
The relevant sub-critical and service-regime boundaries are approximately 600°C and 700–750°C, respectively.
